For I did not discuss them in such a way as to affirm that some exist, or to prove through adduced arguments that it is likely. On the contrary, I said that I would refrain from writing more about the kind of astronomy that would exist for the inhabitants of Saturn, precisely because most people consider it too absurd for men to live on planets; and therefore, they would say that I was wasting my time investigating what those might observe who do not exist in the nature of things. However, when I named the months of the Saturnians while calculating the period of the Saturnian Moon, I did nothing new or unusual for astronomers, for whom nothing is more common than to imagine that someone exists on the Sun or Moon, and from there observes the motions of the stars. There was no reason for Fabrius to blame me for having proposed this invention about Saturnians there. And even if it were otherwise, I would be neither the first to have put this forward, nor would it be so ridiculous, at least among philosophers, as he thinks. But I shall not digress into these matters beyond my established purpose. The contemplation of the Fabrian System calls me, namely that one by which, after he demolished mine, he trusts that the phenomena around Saturn can be conveniently explained. For those earlier arguments, by which he attempts to order the motion of Saturn itself with new laws, are irrelevant here, and it would not be worth the effort to examine them. I wonder, however, what displeased him in the Tychonic hypothesis, to make him decide to build a new one from its foundations: one which I fear astronomers can hardly grasp, let alone approve.

And from all these is gathered the necessity of administration, which may conform to the intention, and lead it to effect, and preserve it; and it is taught that a principality, just like a single spirit, and the art of ruling, is required no less than in a physical body, that of one man. Reason in the soul and the intellect of things to be done, and those which must be commanded to be executed by individual members. The members of one man are not suitable for all actions, but must be preserved and informed under their own. The foot cannot see, the eye cannot walk, the ear cannot touch, the hand cannot hear, because it does not have the instrument or organ for that. Nor does the soul, which knows the faculty and action of each member, command the same things, but its own proper things, and thus it cares entirely for each with its own proper care, an example of which the prudent administration that presides over the body of society follows, and foresees and provides for what is convenient for each member or man. First and especially it regards the whole body of the people, then also individuals: lest while it only considers the whole, with the parts despised, from which the whole is perfected, the whole itself may fail.

VII. Q. *An Genus in communi, univoce predicetur de Genere entis realis, & entis rationis?* Respondeo. Haec duo Genera secundum suas partes materiales tantum convenire inter se analogice; quia Ens tantum analogice potest praedicari de ente reali, & ente rationis. At vero si in esse generis, & prout sunt considerationis Logicae accipiantur; cum utriusque idem prorsus sit artificium Logicum, & conceptus, dubium non esse, quia univoce inter se conveniant.

VIII. Q. *Cum Genus summum ab infimo aeque multum distet, quam Genus infimum a Specie; cur Genus infimum aliud est universale, quam species; & Genus summum non aliud, quam genus infimum?* Respondeo. Diversitatem istam non petendam esse a majori vel minori distantia, quam universalia habent in linea praedicamentali; sed ab eorum conceptu quidditativo. Cum itaque & Genus summum, & Genus infimum praedicentur ut pars materialis; species vero, ut tota essentia; dubium esse nullum potest, quin species a Genere infimo plus differat, quam hoc a summo.

IX. Q. *An conceptus definiens Genus signatum sit conceptus faciens formaliter Genus exercitum?* Respondeo. Cum conceptus faciens Genus in actu exercito debeat etiam facere universale in actu exercito; universale autem fieri non possit per conceptum simplicem non abstrahentem a multitudine; & conceptus definiens Genus signatum non abstrahat a multitudine; sicut est conceptus simplex, ita non est conceptus faciens Genus in actu exercito. Per definitionem itaque Generis definitur Genus signate, non autem fit exercite.

X. Q. *Quid sit species in communi sumpta?* Respondeo. Etsi certum sit, speciem metaphysicam sumptam in communi recte posse dici, *Unum aptum inesse multis ut tota essentia*; ingens tamen inter hanc & speciem Logicam cum sit discrimen, non immerito quaeri posset, an cum Logicum universale sit praedicabile, Speciei Logicae dari possit definitio in communi? VII. Question. *Is Genus in common predicated univocally of the Genus of real being and of being of reason?* I answer. These two Genera agree among themselves analogically only according to their material parts; because Being can only be predicated analogically of real being and of being of reason. But if they are taken in the being of genus, and as they are of logical consideration, since the logical artifice and concept of both is absolutely the same, there is no doubt that they agree among themselves univocally.

VIII. Question. *Since the highest Genus is as far removed from the lowest as the lowest Genus is from the Species; why is the lowest Genus a different universal than the species; and the highest Genus not different from the lowest genus?* I answer. This diversity is not to be sought from the greater or lesser distance that universals have in the predicamental line; but from their quidditative concept. Since, therefore, both the highest Genus and the lowest Genus are predicated as a material part; the species, however, as the whole essence; there can be no doubt that the species differs more from the lowest Genus than this does from the highest.

IX. Question. *Is the concept defining the signed Genus the concept making the exercised Genus?* I answer. Since the concept making a Genus in the exercised act <note>original: "in actu exercito"</note> must also make a universal in the exercised act; but a universal cannot be created by a simple concept not abstracting from a multitude; and the concept defining the signed Genus <note>original: "Genus signatum"</note> does not abstract from a multitude, as it is a simple concept, so it is not a concept making Genus in the exercised act. Therefore, by the definition of Genus, Genus is defined in the signed way, but it is not created in the exercised way.

X. Question. *What is species taken in common?* I answer. Although it is certain that a metaphysical species taken in common can rightly be called, *One apt to be in many as the whole essence*; nevertheless, since there is a great difference between this and a Logical species, it could not unfairly be asked whether, since a Logical universal is predicable, a definition in common can be given to a Logical Species? Hence, there is everywhere a deep silence among authors regarding this definition, always defining species either as only predicable, or as only subjectible. We think, therefore, that for a Species taken in common, as it includes the Predicable and the subjectible, no better definition can be given than this: (*One apt to terminate a proposition as the whole essence*). The Relations that we report here are drawn from a manuscript of the Library of the Count of Seignelay, and are the work of two Arab merchants, the first of whom traveled to China in the year 237 of the Hijra, that is to say, the year 861 of Christ; the other in 264 of the aforementioned Hijra, that is, 877 of the Christian Era. The first of these Relations is missing its beginning, and is also mutilated in the middle: the other is whole, and bears the name of the Arab Author, who is Abuzeid el Hasen of Siraf. They deserve much esteem, both for their antiquity, and for the simplicity with which they are written, and for the abundance of rare news that they contain within themselves. Everyone knows that the first Writer who treated of China with some foundation was Marco Polo the Venetian, who returned from his Travels in the East in the year 1295, whence the relation of these two Arabs boasts 400 years of antiquity over him. They are eyewitnesses, and in such a manner, without trickery or affectation, they narrate the things seen by them that they command complete faith. There are so many particularities that they describe, both regarding the quality of the country and concerning the customs of the Chinese, that delight results equal to the utility. See how the drink of Tea is described to us: "They call it Sah, and it is a small shrub that gives more leaves than the pomegranate tree, and whose odor is more pleasant, but which tastes a bit bitter. Water is boiled and poured over the leaf; and this drink makes them recover from every ailment." Of Porcelain, then, it is spoken of as follows: "They have a precious earth, whence they form vessels, which for delicacy and transparency resemble those of glass."
